title: Unpaid, not unvalued
hook: caring, housework and volunteering are work, and traditions honor them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hospital cleaners who reshaped their own jobs, and Herbert's line about sweeping a room. Your line was craft the job. What did you reshape? Today, the work nobody pays for at all. Day nine hundred twelve.

Who washed the dishes after dinner last night? Who sat up with the feverish child, drove the grandparent to the appointment, folded the laundry, coached the team, made the casserole for the neighbor after the funeral? None of it shows up on a paycheck. When someone asks, so what do you do, almost none of it gets mentioned. And yet a household, a street, a congregation would start to fall apart without it. Today: unpaid, not unvalued.
screen: `DISHES, FEVERS, RIDES, CASSEROLES.` → `NOT ON ANY PAYCHECK.` → `WITHOUT IT, THINGS FALL APART.`

segments.voice: First, a name for it. Unpaid work is still work. Caring for children or the sick, keeping a home running, volunteering: they take time, skill and energy, just like paid jobs. The only thing missing is the money, and money is not the only measure of worth. Second, a very old portrait. The last chapter of the book of Proverbs, in the Hebrew Bible, praises a capable woman. Much of what it honors is the work of a household: she rises while it's still night, provides food, makes cloth, opens her hand to the poor. One verse says, "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." In some Jewish homes, this poem is sung at the Friday night table. Housework, in that text, is not invisible. It's sung about. Third, a word from Sikh tradition: seva, selfless service. At a gurdwara, the Sikh place of worship, volunteers cook and serve langar, a free communal meal open to anyone who walks in. Others wash the dishes, sweep the floors, or care for visitors' shoes. Nobody is paid. In Sikh teaching, this is not a lesser task than worship; seva is itself a way of serving God and the community, and anyone may take part, whatever their standing. Fourth, what this asks of us. If unpaid work is real work, then the people doing it deserve real thanks. Not a vague nod at holidays, but a specific word: I saw what you did, and it mattered. That kind of noticing costs nothing, and it can be given tonight.
screen: `UNPAID WORK IS STILL WORK.` · `THE BREAD OF IDLENESS.` · `SEVA, SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `I SAW WHAT YOU DID.` · then, large: `UNPAID, NOT UNVALUED.`

segments.voice: Let the unpaid work around you come into view, for these two minutes. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind a meal someone cooked for you, a bed someone made, a ride someone gave, a hard day someone sat through with you. Let one person stand out. See their hands doing the work. Then let your own unpaid work come to mind, too, the things you do that nobody counts. Hold both without a ledger. If you pray, you can hold that person in your tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Unpaid. Work done without wages, caring, housework, volunteering, that is still real work, and honored in the old texts and traditions. Today's word.
Your line: unpaid, not unvalued. Today, thank one person for a specific piece of unpaid work they do. Name the work, not just the person. Day nine hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Sikhs perform seva at gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, cleaning and caring for visitors; in some Jewish homes the poem from Proverbs 31 is sung at the Friday night table.

notes: A Jewish reviewer should confirm the framing that Eshet Chayil (Proverbs 31:10–31) is sung at the Friday night table 'in many homes'.

A Sikh Keeper should confirm the description of seva and langar, including 'people of every rank do it' and that seva is understood as serving God and the community; and confirm the Gurmukhi ਸੇਵਾ and pronunciation.
The KJV calls the woman 'a virtuous woman' (31:10); the script says 'a capable woman' in its own words.
